newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's miners on strike over wages, talks fail.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's miners on strike over wages, talks fail.

text.p: About 1,000 Ukrainian miners picketed President Leonid Kuchma's administration building on Wednesday demanding months of back wages, but the country's top security official said talks with the strikers had collapsed.

The miners, chanting "Pay! Pay!", ripped their pit helmets from their heads and threw them on the ground. "Mr. President, give us our money back," read one placard as police barred pedestrians from passing in front of Kuchma's offices.
The Coal Ministry said 43 mines were on strike, more than double last week's figure. Independent trade unions put it at 50 pits. There are approximately 1,000 miners per pit on average.
Ukraine has 250 mines, so old and inefficient that despite low local wages it is cheaper to import coal than use what is produced at home. Most pits are in the eastern Donbass region.

"The strike will go on and the number of striking pits will increase," said Yuri Berdnyk, leader of the independent miners' trade union. "It seems the government cannot meet our main demand to pay the 1.4 billion hryvnias ($760 million) owed us."

Regular strikes protesting low pay, no pay, and unsafe working conditions have taken place for at least a decade, but the number of strikers in the last week is greater than usual as Ukraine struggles to shrink its growing wage debt mountain.

"The situation in the coal-mining industry is difficult," Volodymyr Horbulin, secretary of the policy-making Security and Defence Council, told a news conference after morning talks with miners' leaders which failed to reach a compromise.
"My arguments at meetings with miners to stop such strikes failed," he said. "This industry creates problems for our country. I cannot say we found ways how to deal with it. New ways must be found."
Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko started another round of talks with the miners later on Wednesday.
Ukraine's unpaid wages owed to teachers, doctors, students and pensioners -- some of whom have not been paid in a year -- stands at about four billion hryvnias ($2.2 billion).
"We cannot concentrate exclusively on miners, giving them everything, otherwise we'll face similar actions by shipbuilders or teachers, and so on," Horbulin said.
Berdnyk said the miners had only economic demands but some protesters' slogans in the picket demanded the resignation of the government and president, whose term ends in 1999.
Last year coal output stood at 70.3 million tonnes compared to 83.7 million tonnes in 1995.

The death rate through accidents is the highest of any Ukrainian industry, with 134 miners killed since the begining of the year including two this week at a mine in the eastern town of Rovenki on the Russian border.
A government programme foresees the closure of 80 mines by 2000, helped by a $100 million loan from the World Bank.

But Horbulin warned the reform programme could not entirely solve the industry's problems. "Experience has shown there was not enough money to cover the cost of the last five or seven closures," Horbulin said. "In this way we cannot avoid strikes."
